---
title: "The machine underneath"
---

{{< include ../_setup.qmd >}}

This appendix answers the questions a technical reader asks of any table
tool: where the work happens, when it happens, who optimizes it, and what
happens when the data outgrows the machine. The short answer to all four is
one sentence: god compiles, and an engine executes.

## One engine does the work

A pipeline here is compiled into a single query, about five milliseconds of
work, and the query is executed by software built for executing queries:
DuckDB on this machine, Spark SQL or a warehouse wherever
[Somewhere else](../chapters/somewhere-else.qmd) points. god never touches a
row. It owns the sentence, the checking, and the writing out; the scanning,
joining and grouping are the engine's, which is why
[the appendix on speed](g-where-the-speed-lives.qmd) credits the engine by
name.

The whole pipeline reaches the engine as one query, never a step at a time:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
show_as(sales |>
  keep(region == "West") |>
  add(margin = revenue - cost) |>
  summarize(margin = total(margin), by = product) |>
  sort(descending(margin)) |>
  take(10), "sql")
```

### Python

```{python}
show_as(sales
  >> keep(col.region == "West")
  >> add(margin = col.revenue - col.cost)
  >> summarize(margin = total(col.margin), by = col.product)
  >> sort(descending(col.margin))
  >> take(10), "sql")
```

:::

Five steps, one text. The engine sees the whole question before it reads a
single row.

## Always lazy, one surface

Some tools keep two interfaces: an eager one that runs each step as it is
typed, and a lazy one that plans. god has one, and it is the lazy one. A
verb returns a plan, printing runs it, and `collect` hands over the table,
which is the whole of
[Nothing runs until you ask](../chapters/nothing-runs-yet.qmd). There is no
eager mode to be caught in by accident, and the difference is not cosmetic:
an engine given steps one at a time cannot plan across them. The dated
record in [the appendix on speed](g-where-the-speed-lives.qmd) carries an
eager and a lazy spelling of the same library, and the gap between them is
the price of running step by step.

## What the engine optimizes

Because the query arrives whole, the planning belongs to the engine: which
filter to push into which scan, which join to run first, which columns never
to read at all. Those are decades of database work, and god's job is to stay
out of their way. The steps it writes are flattened by the engine into one
plan, so a pipeline of eight steps is not eight passes over the data.
Nothing about this needed a word in the vocabulary, which is the point: the
grammar buys the optimizer by handing over text.

## When the data outgrows the machine

Two sizes of big, two answers.

A table bigger than memory, held as a frame: the engine can spill its work
to disk, but a pipeline here begins at a table the host already holds, so on
one machine the frame itself is the ceiling. god has no word for reading a
file into a pipeline, and [the coverage appendix](e-coverage.qmd) records
that gap beside the others, with what to do today.

A table bigger than the machine: that is what
[Somewhere else](../chapters/somewhere-else.qmd) is for. The table stays in
the warehouse or on the cluster, the sentence goes there as text, and no
data moves at all. At that size the honest question is not whether one
process can stream one file, and the grammar's answer is to run where the
data lives.

One more property falls out of compiling to text: everything above is
inspectable. `show_as` prints the exact query the engine will run, and the
same pipeline in five libraries beside it, so nothing on this page is taken
on faith.
